subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Status Quo Bias
description: A fast breakdown of Status Quo Bias for builders.

hook.text: Employees keep the same health plan for decades despite better options because switching feels risky.

buildup.text: Samuelson and Zeckhauser found a strong preference for the current state in all kinds of decisions.

discovery.text: Status quo bias: any change involves potential losses that loom larger than potential gains. So we stay put.

twist.text: The status quo often isn't a deliberate choice. It's what happened by default, and now inertia holds it in place.

climax.text: Ask: if I didn't already have this, would I choose it today? If not, the status quo is costing you.

punchline.text: Staying put is also a decision. Own it.

quiz.question: What drives status quo bias?
options: The current option is always the best
Potential losses from change loom larger than potential gains

details.summary: Status quo bias is the strong preference for the current state of affairs, where any change from the baseline is perceived as a loss. People stick with default options, existing products, and current arrangements even when alternatives are objectively better.
details.whyItMatters: Status quo bias explains why people stay with bad insurance plans, expensive banks, and suboptimal investments. Loss aversion makes the potential downsides of switching feel larger than the potential upsides, paralyzing change.
takeaways: Deviation from the status quo is perceived as a risky loss
Defaults are powerful because changing them requires overcoming status quo bias
Businesses exploit status quo bias through auto-renewal and defaults

faq.question: How do companies exploit status quo bias?
faq.answer: Auto-renewal subscriptions, opt-out rather than opt-in enrollment, and pre-selected options all exploit status quo bias. Once set as the default, customers rarely change even when better alternatives exist because changing feels risky.

faq.question: How is status quo bias related to loss aversion?
faq.answer: The current state becomes the reference point. Any change risks losses from leaving the known situation, and loss aversion makes those potential losses feel twice as significant as the potential gains from switching.
